facts.statement: Born at Sydenham on 10 December 1869; studied at the City of London School and Balliol College, Oxford, and became a fellow of Pembroke College in 1893.
Joined the Daily Mail in 1896 and reported from the United States, Greece and the Sudan.
Accompanied Kitchener’s army in 1898 and published With Kitchener to Khartum that year.
Reported the siege of Ladysmith and died there on 15 January 1900.

en.tagline: A correspondent on the road to Khartum.
en.intro: George Warrington Steevens moved from classical scholarship to reporting the world at speed. In 1898 the Daily Mail correspondent followed the Anglo-Egyptian army into the Sudan and wrote the campaign as he saw it.
en.orientation: His account brings the railway, the river and the men of the army into the same story as the battles of the Atbara and Omdurman.
origin: Born in Sydenham in 1869, Steevens attended the City of London School and Balliol College, Oxford. He took first-class honours in classics and became a fellow of Pembroke College in 1893.
career: He joined the Daily Mail in 1896. Assignments took him to the United States and to the Greco-Turkish War before he accompanied Kitchener’s army in the Sudan. In 1899 he reported from India and Rennes, then travelled to South Africa.
During the siege of Ladysmith he contracted enteric fever. He died there on 15 January 1900, before the town was relieved.
literature: With Kitchener to Khartum grew from Steevens’s dispatches and appeared in 1898. His account moves between the mechanics of an expedition and the experience of those who marched and fought in it.
en.legacy: Steevens left the record of a correspondent close to events, writing under the pressures of a newspaper age.
en.bridge: With Kitchener to Khartum follows the advance along the Nile to the battles and the city that gave the book its title.
en.description: George Warrington Steevens (1869–1900), journalist and war correspondent, and author of With Kitchener to Khartum.
